title: Does it make sense to combine statins with other lipid-altering agents following AIM-HIGH, SHARP and ACCORD?
text_summary: 本研究旨在探讨在AIM-HIGH、SHARP和ACCORD试验之后，联合使用他汀类药物与其他降脂药物是否合理。研究发现，虽然多种降脂药物对脂质亚类的影响各不相同，但联合不同药物类别似乎是一种有前景的方法。然而，当与单用他汀类药物相比时，大多数联合用药并未显示出额外的临床益处。进一步的研究导致了多种新型降脂药物的开发，其中一些药物具有非常令人鼓舞的初步结果。鉴于相当一部分患者在使用他汀类药物单药治疗时无法达到指南推荐的脂质水平，联合降脂疗法是一种有前景的下一步，可能成为标准治疗方案。如果未来指南建议将LDL-C的目标水平降至更低，联合疗法的概念可能变得更加重要。然而，每种新药都必须在联合他汀类药物的背景下证明可以降低临床事件。在可预见的未来，HPS2-THRIVE（烟酸）、IMPROVE-IT（依泽替米）、HPS-3 REVEAL TIMI 55（安塞曲普利）和PCSK9单克隆抗体III期临床试验的结果将有助于进一步阐明这一领域的方向。

STATIN DRUGS (MB CLEARFIELD, SECTION EDITOR)
Does it Make Sense to Combine Statins with Other Lipid-Altering
Agents Following AIM-HIGH, SHARP and ACCORD?
Willibald Hochholzer & Robert P. Giugliano
Published online: 16 December 2012
# Springer Science+Business Media New York 2012
Abstract Hypercholesterolemia is one of the main risk
factors for the development of atherosclerotic diseases. Mul-
tiple clinical trials of lipid-lowering agents have demonstrat-
ed that lowering cholesterol effectively reduces the risk of
cardiovascular events and death. Currently, treatment with
3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase inhibi-
tors (“statins”) is the most commonly used approach, given
their superior efficacy relative to other cholesterol lowering
agents. However, not all patients on statin monotherapy
achieve target cholesterol levels, and even when cholesterol
lowering is successful, significant residual cardiovascular
risk remains. There is increasing interest in developing
combination cholesterol-modifying therapies that may aug-
ment the treatment effect and minimize the side effects of
statins. Although there is currently no evidence that any of
the potential therapy combinations can improve clinical
outcome compared to statin monotherapy alone, results of
several large ongoing trials will help to clarify this important
field.
Keywords Lipids . Cholesterol . Cardiovascular risk . Lipid
lowering therapy . Statins . Niacin . Fibrate . Ezetimibe .
Omega-3 fatty acids . Cholesterol ester transfer protein
inhibitors . Proprotein convertase subtilisin kexin type 9
inhibitors
Introduction
Hyperlipidemia is one of the main risk factors for the
development of atherosclerosis, which includes coronary
heart disease (CHD), cerebrovascular disease, and periph-
eral arterial disease [1–4]. In particular, low-density lipo-
protein cholesterol (LDL-C) plays a central role in the
pathophysiology of atherosclerosis, and levels>200 mg/
dL are strongly associated with a higher risk for CHD [5,
6]. Oxidized LDL-C, together with pro-inflammatory
mediators produced by enzymes binding to LDL-C, trig-
gers inflammatory processes leading to the development
of atherosclerotic atheroma and plaque rupture [7]. Mul-
tiple clinical trials of lipid-lowering agents have demon-
strated that lowering LDL-C effectively reduces the risk
of cardiovascular events and death in patients with and
without CHD [1, 8•]. Therefore, lowering LDL-C is a
major cornerstone for both primary and secondary pre-
vention of cardiovascular events.
Epidemiological studies have also suggested that low
levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C)
are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular
events [9]. Imaging studies have demonstrated regres-
sion of atherosclerosis with HDL-C increasing strategies
[10, 11], but large randomized trials have failed so far
to demonstrate a significant effect of HDL-C modifying
strategies on clinical outcome [12••]. An association
with cardiovascular events that is less clear than for
LDL-C and HDL-C has also been described for trigly-
cerides, small dense lipoprotein subfractions, and lipo-
protein a [9, 13].
Several lipid-lowering drugs with variable effects on lipid
subclasses became clinically available over the last decades
or are currently under investigation (Table 1). Given the
varying effects of the different drugs on lipid subclasses,
combining different drug classes appears to be a promising
approach.

Target Levels of Blood Lipids: Current
Recommendations and Future Directions
In western populations, total cholesterol has a normal distri-
bution with a median level of ~200 mg/dL [6, 14]. Since a
significant proportion of these populations develop athero-
sclerosis, including even apparently healthy individuals with
total cholesterol and LDL-C levels below the median, these
levels should not be considered as normal [5, 15]. In patients
at high risk for CHD or with known CHD, results of large
trials evaluating lipid-lowering therapies have shown that
aiming for LDL-C levels of ~100 mg/dL or even well below
100 mg/dL can only prevent 20–25 % of subsequent CHD
events [16–19]. Therefore, in persons at high risk for the
development of CHD or in patients with established CHD,
current North American and European guidelines recommend
an LDL-C goal of less than 100 mg/dL, with an optional goal
of<70 mg/dL in patients at highest risk [20•, 21, 22•]. In
patients at lower risk for CHD, the LDL-C goals are consid-
erable higher (e.g., < 190 mg/dL for those at lowest risk).
Since patients with LDL-C levels well below 100 mg/dL
still are at risk for CHD events, it has been proposed that the
optimal LDL-C level should be that level at which no clini-
cally significant atherosclerosis develops [5, 6]. A recent
meta-analysis tried to determine which LDL-C levels would
be needed to reach this goal [23]. In this analysis, a linear
correlation of progression of atherosclerosis and LDL-C levels
was found—irrespective of if patients were on statin therapy
or placebo. The calculated threshold of LDL-C to minimize
recurrent cardiovascular events was ~57 mg/dL for primary
prevention and even lower (~30 mg/dL) for secondary pre-
vention, regardless of the presence of other risk factors. Up-
coming large randomized trials of lipid-lowering therapies,
such as IMProved Reduction of Outcomes: Vytorin Efficacy
International Trial (IMPROVE-IT), will finally answer the
question if “even lower is even better” (i.e., if an LDL of
50–55 mg/dL will translate into fewer cardiovascular events
compared to an LDL of 65–70 mg/dL) [24]. Thus, LDL-C
goals of future guidelines might become even lower than the
currently recommended levels.
While cut-offs and treatment recommendations are well
defined for LDL-C, they are not as clear for other blood
lipids. HDL-C levels of below 40 mg/dL and triglyceride
levels of more than 150 mg/dL are associated with an
increased risk for cardiovascular events [4, 25]. However,
results of clinical studies specifically investigating the
effects of lipid-modifying strategies on these particular lipid
subgroups are very limited. For HDL-C, observational data
as well as clinical studies investigating surrogate endpoints
have suggested that raising HDL-C may reduce cardiovas-
cular events [10, 26], but the first large randomized trial of
the modern era enrolling patients with low HDL-C and
investigating a HDL-C modifying therapy could not dem-
onstrate an effect on clinical outcome [12••]. Recent data on
genetic mechanisms that raise HDL-C also challenge the
concept that raising HDL-C will translate into a lower risk
for cardiovascular events [27•]. Therefore, it remains un-
clear if drugs modifying HDL-C and triglyceride levels
should be recommended as general approach. Further pro-
spective studies identifying target levels and treatment strat-
egies that improve clinical outcome are needed.
Limitations of Lipid Modifying Monotherapy
Modification of diet, as part of a “therapeutic lifestyle
change,” is considered the first recommendation for patients
with suboptimal lipid profiles. Large controlled studies have
shown that a reduction of cardiovascular events can be
achieved with lipid-lowering diets [28]. However, poor ad-
herence to low fat/cholesterol diets is one of the major
limitations of these interventions. Furthermore, the clinical

benefit of low fat/cholesterol diets may be blunted in some
patients by genetic differences of lipid metabolism [29],
such that the majority of patients achieve only modest
(~10 %) reductions in LDL-C with diet therapy alone [30].
Another potential approach for lipid-lowering is bariatric
surgery. Over 20 years ago, the Program on Surgical Control
of Hyperlipidemia (POSCH) trial demonstrated that ileal
bypass surgery can produce a 35 % reduction in LDL-C,
which was associated with a 24 % reduction in cardiovas-
cular events after 5 years [31]. A similar trend was seen in
more recent studies [32, 33]. However, the limitations of
such a treatment are obvious.
Current treatment guidelines for lipid-modifying drugs fo-
cus on LDL-C reduction as the primary goal of therapy [3, 4,
22•]. 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase
inhibitors (“statins”) are considered as standard of care, given
their superior efficacy relative to other LDL-C lowering agents
and overwhelming evidence of both secondary and primary
prevention of cardiovascular events [3, 4, 22•]. With the advent
of more potent statins, an LDL-C reduction of up to 60 %
appears to be possible [19, 34–37]. In large trials of potent
statins, the majority of patients achieved LDL-C levels below
100 mg/dL, with mean LDL-C levels in recent large random-
ized trials between 55 and 80 mg/dL [19, 35–37]. However,
these results are often not seen in clinical routine, since most
trials excluded patients with very high lipid levels, insufficient
LDL-C reduction or intertolerance to statin therapy.
Therefore, not all patients on statin monotherapy achieve
the guideline recommended LDL-C levels. Increasing the
dose of a statin may not be sufficient in a significant pro-
portion of patients, since doubling of statin dose results only
in a 5–7 % additional reduction in LDL-C [34]. Even when
target LDL-C levels are achieved, patients are still at signif-
icant residual cardiovascular risk [8•, 16, 19, 38]. Other
limitations are the potential adverse effects of statins, with
liver and muscle toxicity as the major adverse effects [39,
40]. These side effects of statins appear to be dose related
and not associated with the on-treatment LDL-C level.
However, most patients tolerate statin therapy well, even
when very low LDL-C levels are attained [41, 42]. For
patients that cannot tolerate currently available statins, a
novel statin with enhanced liver extraction and reduced
plasma exposure is currently being compared in a trial
versus atorvastatin in statin-intolerant patients (PPD10558,
Furiex Pharmaceuticals, Morrisville, NC) [43]. Another lim-
itation of statins is that their principal effect is to lower
LDL-C levels. Although statins also reduce triglycerides
and increase HDL-C through independent mechanisms,
these effects are only modest at best [34].
For these reasons, there is increasing interest in develop-
ing combination LDL-C-lowering therapies that may aug-
ment the treatment effect and minimize the side effects of
statins.
Current Data for Lipid-Modifying Combination Therapies:
Not Every Approach Improves Outcome
Omega-3 Fatty Acids
Omega-3 fatty acids, such as docosahexaenoic acid (DHA)
and eicosapenatenoic acid (EPA), have been shown to reduce
triglycerides in a dose dependent manner, but effects on LDL-
C and HDL-C vary between negligible to moderate, with
some preparations even slightly increasing levels of LDL-C
[44]. Results of prospective cohort studies and trials demon-
strated that 250 mg/day of DHA and/or EPA can reduce the
risk of coronary death by 36 % [45]. However, in most
randomized trials evaluating omega-3 fatty acids, only a lim-
ited proportion of patients were treated with a statin [46, 47].
Recent trials evaluating omega-3 fatty acids in addition to
statin treatment demonstrated no further reduction of cardio-
vascular events by adding omega-3 fatty acids [48, 49], or at
most, only a modest benefit [50]. Recently published data
suggest a significant interaction of the treatment effect of
omega-3 fatty acids with statin use, leading to no further
reduction of cardiovascular events if omega-3 fatty acids are
added to statin therapy [51].
Fibrates
Fibrates lower triglycerides by 20–50 % and LDL-C by up to
20 %, while raising HDL-C by 0–15 % by interacting with the
genetic expression of apolipoproteins A1 and A2, lipoprotein
lipase, apolipoprotein C-3, and acute phase proteins [52, 53]. A
recent meta-analysis also showed a lowering effect on LDL-C
[54•]. When used as monotherapy, fibrates can reduce cardio-
vascular events by 10–15 %. Some studies suggested that this
effect might be even more pronounced in patients with low
HDL-C and elevated triglycerides; however, this could not be
confirmed in other analyses [54•].
The first generation of fibrates raised concerns about
potential toxicity [55]. Further analyses showed an in-
creased risk of rhabdomyolysis, particularly when gemfi-
brozil was used in combination with statins [56]. However,
newer fibrates such as fenofibrate did not show these safety
signals, even when used together with statins [57••].
Several large-scale trials of fibrate therapy have been com-
pleted in the past few years. Among these, only the Action to
Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes (ACCORD) trial
[57••] evaluated fibrates with routine statin therapy in all
enrolled patients. Therefore, this trial is particularly pertinent
to clinical practice. ACCORD compared fenofibrate in com-
bination with simvastatin compared to simvastatin alone in
patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus who were at high risk for
cardiovascular events. The primary endpoint was the first
occurrence of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke,
or death from cardiovascular causes during mean follow-up of

4.7 years. The additional use of fenofibrate did not reduce the
primary endpoint or any of the secondary endpoints, despite
achieving a 2 % increase in HDL-C and a 15 % decrease in
triglyceride levels.
Niacin
Nicotinic acid, or niacin, has been used to lower cholesterol
since the 1950’s [58, 59]. In addition to its LDL-C lowering
effects [60], niacin is the most effective available agent for
raising HDL-C [4, 61]. Studies such as the Coronary Drug
Project, conducted from 1966 to 1975, showed a significant
risk reduction for myocardial infarction and stroke with
niacin monotherapy [59, 62].
Unfortunately, despite its long history in clinical use,
limited data are available regarding the clinical benefit of
niacin in combination with other agents. Recently, the Athe-
rothrombosis Intervention in Metabolic syndrome with low
HDL-C/high triglycerides: Impact on Global Health out-
comes trial (AIM-HIGH) was stopped 18 months earlier
than planned by the independent Data Safety Committee
because of futility [12••]. This randomized trial enrolled
3,414 patients in the United States and Canada with estab-
lished cardiovascular disease and atherogenic dyslipidemia.
Patients were randomized to treatment with either extended-
release niacin (1.5–2.0 g/day) or placebo in addition to
simvastatin or simvastatin plus ezetimibe (10 mg/day) to
achieve a goal LDL-C in the range of 40–80 mg/dL. The
primary efficacy outcome was time to first cardiovascular
event, defined as the composite of CHD death, nonfatal
myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, hospitalization for
acute coronary syndrome, or symptom-driven coronary or
cerebral revascularization. The combination of extended-
release niacin and a statin increased HDL-C and lowered
triglyceride levels compared to statin alone, but the addition
of niacin did not reduce clinical endpoints. There was even a
small increase in ischemic stroke rate in the niacin group
(niacin: 1.7 %; control 1.1 %, p00.11). However, it remains
unclear whether this was an arbitrary finding, since nine of the
29 strokes in the niacin group occurred in patients who had
discontinued niacin at least two months before their stroke.
The Treatment of HDL-C to Reduce the Incidence of
Vascular Events (HPS2-THRIVE) trial evaluating the clinical
efficacy of niacin therapy has completed enrollment in over
25,000 patients and results are expected in early 2013 [63].
Patients with a history of cardiovascular disease (prior myo-
cardial infarction, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral vascular
disease, or diabetes with symptomatic CHD) already on in-
tensive LDL-C-lowering therapy with high-dose simvastatin
or simvastatin/ezetimibe were randomized to extended-release
niacin plus laropiprant, a selective prostaglandin-2 receptor
inhibitor that reduces prostaglandin-mediated flushing, or pla-
cebo. The primary efficacy outcome of HPS2-THRIVE is
time to first cardiovascular event, a composite of coronary
death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and
requirement for arterial revascularization. This trial will help
to clarify whether aggressive HDL-C-raising with niacin can
improve cardiovascular outcomes beyond what is already
achieved with intensive statin monotherapy. Preliminary data
on safety was reported at the European Society of Cardiology
Congress in August 2012, and revealed an incidence of my-
opathy of 0.5 % in patients treated with simvastatin 40 mg and
niacin plus laropiprant [64]. However, the vast majority of
these cases were observed in patients of Chinese descent.
Ezetimibe
Ezetimibe is a cholesterol absorption inhibitor that inhibits
duodenal Niemann-Pick C1-like protein 1 [65], and reduces
LDL-C by 15–20 % in addition to statin [10, 65, 66, 67••].
Following mixed results of surrogate marker studies [10,
65], two randomized trials investigated the effect of ezeti-
mibe combined with simvastatin versus placebo on clinical
endpoints: The Simvastatin and Ezetimibe in Aortic Steno-
sis (SEAS) trial enrolled 1,873 patients with mild-to-
moderate, asymptomatic aortic stenosis [66]. Treatment with
simvastatin plus ezetimibe compared to placebo significant-
ly reduced the incidence of the secondary endpoint of is-
chemic cardiovascular events by 22 %, but did not affect the
primary endpoint (composite outcome of combined aortic-
valve events and ischemic events).
In the Study of Heart and Renal Protection (SHARP),
9,270 patients with chronic kidney disease with no known
history of myocardial infarction or coronary revascularization
were randomly assigned to simvastatin plus ezetimibe versus
placebo. The primary endpoint of non-fatal myocardial infarc-
tion or coronary death, non-hemorrhagic stroke, or any arterial
revascularization procedure was significantly reduced by
treatment with simvastatin plus ezetimibe (13.4 % vs.
11.3 %, p00.002) [67••]. Also, the combination of primary
endpoint plus non-coronary cardiac deaths and hemorrhagic
strokes was significantly reduced (17.6 % vs. 15.1 %, p0
0.001). Therapy with simvastatin plus ezetimibe compared
to placebo was not associated with a higher incidence of
cancer, myopathy or hepatic adverse events. These results
are noteworthy, since previous trials with high-potent statins
in the setting of chronic (pre-)terminal kidney disease could
not demonstrate a reduction of cardiovascular events [68, 69].
However, despite the fact that ezetimibe has now been
used in clinical routine for almost a decade, no trial has
demonstrated the benefit of this drug on the background of
statin therapy. The IMProved Reduction of Outcomes:
Vytorin Efficacy International Trial (IMPROVE-IT) will
help to clarify this important question [24]. This trial en-
rolled over 18,000 stabilized patients within 10 days follow-
ing an acute coronary syndrome, and randomized them to

ezetimibe or placebo on a background of high-dose simvas-
tatin treatment. Results of this trial are expected in 2014.
Upcoming Trials and Promising Novel Therapeutic
Approaches
Since listing of all lipid-modifying drugs in clinical devel-
opment would be beyond the scope of this review, this
section will focus on selected novel approaches with the
potential to become clinically available in near future.
Cholesterol Ester Transfer Protein Inhibitors
Cholesterol ester transfer protein (CETP) facilitates the
transport of cholesterol esters in exchange for triglycerides
between lipoproteins such as LDL-C and HDL-C (Figure)
[70]. Familial CETP deficiency appears not to be harmful
and is associated with considerably increased HDL-C levels
and reduced levels of LDL-C [71].
Torcetrapib was the first CETP inhibitor to undergo clin-
ical investigation (Pfizer, Groton, CT). In early studies, it
reduced LDL-C by 25 % and raised HDL-C by 130 % [72],
and improved glycemic control in patients with type 2
diabetes mellitus [73]. First imaging studies showed only
limited effect of torcetrapib on carotid intima media thick-
ness and atheroma volume [74]. However, a large clinical
outcome study, the Investigation of Lipid Level Manage-
ment to Understand its Impact in Atherosclerotic Events
(ILLUMINATE) trial, was terminated prematurely because
of an increased risk of death and cardiac events in patients
receiving torcetrapib [72]. Subsequent analyses showed that
torcetrapib raised blood pressure [72, 74]. Increased aldo-
sterone, corticosterone and endothelin-1 production were
identified as potential mechanisms for these findings [72,
74]. These off-target effects appear to be unique for torce-
trapib, since they were not seen with other CETP inhibitors
[75, 76•].
Currently, two other CETP inhibitors are being evaluated
in large randomized phase III trials. Dalcetrapib (Hoffman
La Roche, Basel, Switzerland) raises HDL-C by up to 33 %
but has only limited effect on LDL-C [75]. Early studies
demonstrated that this compound is tolerated well, but failed
to demonstrate an effect on endothelial function [77]. An
imaging trial did not show any significant benefits on plaque
composition [78]. The Dal-OUTCOMES phase III trial that
planned to enroll 15,600 patients with acute coronary syn-
dromes was initiated in 2008 [79]. This trial was terminated
early, in May 2012, after an interim analysis showed no
significant effect of dalcetrapib on cardiovascular endpoints.
The preliminary announcement from the sponsor indicated
that there were no safety issues that led to the premature
termination of the trial [80].
Anacetrapib is a third CETP inhibitor, and is currently
being investigated in a large clinical outcome trial [81]. It
raises HDL-C by 90–130 % and reduces LDL-C by 25–
40 % [76•, 82]. Like dalcetrapib, no adverse effects on blood
pressure or other safety parameters were seen in phase II
studies [76•]. The Heart Protection Study 3 - Randomized
EValuation of the Effects of Anacetrapib Through Lipid-
modification Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction 55
(HPS-3 REVEAL TIMI 55) outcome trial initiated in 2011
is currently evaluating anacetrapib when added to baseline
statin therapy in 30,000 patients with established cardiovas-
cular, cerebrovascular, or peripheral arterial disease [81].
First results are expected in 2017.
Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin Kexin Type 9 Inhibitors
Proprotein convertase subtilisin kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a
protein that promotes lysosomal degradation of the LDL-C
receptor and prevents its recycling by transporting back to the
hepatocyte cell surface (Fig. 1) [83]. Thus, PCSK9 down-
regulates the cell-surface expression LDL-C receptor and
decreases removal of LDL-C from the circulation. PCSK9
activity is related to fasting, postprandial lipid metabolism
and hormonal control of lipids [84]. Loss-of-function muta-
tions in PCSK9 gene have been shown to be associated with a
substantial reduction in plasma LDL-C and 50–90 % lifetime
reduced risk of CHD events [85]. Conversely, gain-of-
function mutations in PCSK9 gene cause autosomal dominant
hypercholesterolemia, with elevated LDL-C and associated
premature coronary artery disease [86].
Since low intrahepatocyte levels of cholesterol cause in-
creased expression of the LDL-C receptor and PCSK9 [87],
treatment with potent LDL-C lowering agents that reduce
hepatic cholesterol synthesis (e.g., high-dose statins) might
be counterbalanced by increased PCSK9 expression. Results
from a randomized controlled trial comparing a potent statin
vs. placebo have demonstrated up-regulation of PCSK9 fol-
lowing treatment with high-dose statins [88]. Therefore, inhi-
bition of PCSK9 has the potential to profoundly decrease
circulating LDL-C and might increase potency of statins.
Several injectable antibodies to PCSK9 that increase
expression of the LDL-C receptor and reduce plasma
LDL-C by 40–70 % have been developed in recent years
[89, 90••, 91•, 92•]. Two such monoclonal antibodies,
REGN-727/SAR-236553 (SanofiAventis, Paris, France)
[90••] and AMG-145 (Amgen, Thousand Oaks, CA) [91•],
which are administered subcutaneously every 2–4 weeks,
are beginning phase III clinical trials in late 2012 or early
2013. Phase II data with REGN-727/SAR-236553 demon-
strated LDL-C reductions of up to 72 % in patients already
on statin therapy [92•]. Other approaches (including oral
drugs) to inhibit PCSK9, such as degradation of the PCSK9
mRNA by either small interfering RNA or antisense

oligonucleotides, as well as small molecule inhibitors, also
are under development [93, 94].
Other Compounds
Microsomal transfer protein inhibitors block triglyceride
absorption and chylomicron secretion from the intestine
and very-low-density lipoprotein secretion from the liver
[95]. Since most compounds caused non-alcoholic steatotic
hepatitis by an increase of hepatic cholesterol pools, only
lomitapide (AEGR-733; Aegerion Pharmaceuticals, Cam-
bridge, MA) is currently under further investigation [95].
Thyroid mimetics were already evaluated in The Coro-
nary Drug Project, where dextro (d)-thyroxine reduced
LDL-C but also increased the incidence of arrhythmias,
which led to discontinuation of this arm of the trial [96].
Further research clarified the role of thyroid α- receptors
and β-receptors, and suggested that selective β-agonists
would reduce lipids without any further cardiovascular off-
target effects [96]. Eprotirome (Karo Bio AB; Stockholm,
Sweden) and sobetirome (QuatRx Inc, Ann Arbor, MI) are
currently under investigation and have shown an LDL-C
reduction of up to more than 30 % [97].
Antisense oligonucleotide therapies reduce or silence gene
expression by inactivating messenger RNA with complemen-
tary antisense sequences [98]. Since RNAs are unstable, sev-
eral modifications that protect against degradation, such as
hydrolysis, are needed before they can be used as injectable
drugs [98]. Mipomersen (Isis, Carlsbad,CA and Genzyme,
Cambridge, MA) is the first antisense therapy interfering with
apoB expression evaluated for use in humans [99]. It reduces
LDL-C by up to 35 % with no significant effects on HDL-C
[99]. In patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterol-
emia, mipomersen reduced LDL-C by 25 % when added to
maximum tolerated dose of other lipid-lowering drugs [100].
Main adverse effects of this treatment are injection site reac-
tions and hepatic steatosis [99, 100].
Conclusions
Several lipid-modifying agents have demonstrated a signif-
icant impact on cardiovascular events. However, when used
in combination with statins as the standard of treatment,
most of these compounds failed to show an additional
clinical benefit. Further research has led to the development
of several novel lipid-modifying drugs—some of them with
very promising preliminary results.
Given the fact that a significant proportion of patients do
not achieve guideline recommended lipid levels with statin
monotherapy, combined lipid-lowering therapies are a prom-
ising next step and might become standard of care. The notion
of combination therapy might become even more important if
future guidelines recommend even lower target levels for
LDL-C. However, each new compound would have to dem-

After acceptance of this manuscript results of the dal-OUT-
COMES trial and 4 phase II studies with the PCSK9 inhib-
itor AMG 145 were published. The dal-OUTCOMES study
(GG Schwartz, NEJM 2012 published online, doi:10.1056/
NEJMoa1206797) showed no reduction in cardiovascular
events with dalcetrapib despite raising HDL by 31-40 %
during the trial from the baseline. Four phase II trials with

reduction in LDL-C of 40-66 % in patients with hypercho-
lesterolemia on statin (Giugliano RP, Lancet 2012 published
on-line http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(12)61770-X),

erant patients (Sullivan D, JAMA. 2012;308(23) published

image_summary: Figure 1是一张示意图，展示了肝脏、循环系统和组织中脂蛋白代谢的机制。图中包含肝脏（Liver）、循环（Circulation）、组织（Tissue）等结构，以及PCSK9、LDL - C Receptor（低密度脂蛋白胆固醇受体）、LDL - C（低密度脂蛋白胆固醇）、HDL - C（高密度脂蛋白胆固醇）、CETP（胆固醇酯转运蛋白）、Cholesterol（胆固醇）、Triglycerides（甘油三酯）等关键分子。箭头表示物质运输或分子间相互作用的方向，例如PCSK9与LDL - C受体结合后，可能促进LDL - C受体向溶酶体（Lysosome）降解；CETP介导HDL - C和LDL - C之间的胆固醇与甘油三酯交换；LDL - C和HDL - C在循环系统中运输，组织细胞可摄取LDL - C等，整体呈现脂蛋白代谢的路径和关键分子调控关系。
